title: No, not, not yet, don't have
title_target: មិន … ទេ — min … té
goal: Say no correctly — and accept that Khmer fences off a negative with TWO words at once, where English gets by with one "not".
bekal: negate with មិន … ទេ and អត់ … ទេ
tell apart "not", "not (a thing)", "not yet", and "don't have"
use គ្មាន for "don't have"
turn down an offer gently with អត់អីទេ

dialogs.title: កិច្ចសន្ទនា — The offers keep coming
dialogs.intro: Sokha joins them and starts offering Ani everything — a Cambodian host's habit that won't stop until you accept something. Notice the double fence in each of Ani's negatives: មិន or អត់ in front, ទេ at the end. Drop either one and the sentence limps.

grammars.title: ⚠️ The negative has TWO fences — the number-one beginner mistake
body: English negates with one word: "not". Khmer uses **two words that bracket the sentence**: one before the verb, one at the end. Forgetting the one at the end is the mistake heard most often from learners throughout the first year.
after: មិន is more standard, អត់ more casual. On the streets of Phnom Penh you will hear អត់ far more often; in writing and formal situations, មិន. Both are correct, and both need ទេ at the end.
⚠️ **កុំ (don't) is the only one that doesn't need ទេ.** A prohibition stands on its own: កុំភ្លេច (don't forget), កុំទៅ (don't go). Adding ទេ there is actually wrong.

grammars.title: Four kinds of "no" you must not mix up
body: English mostly gets by with "not" and "no"; Khmer distinguishes four cases, and mixing them up makes you sound odd even when you are understood.

Say it

after: ⚠️ **គ្មាន is the opposite of មាន** (have / there is), not an ordinary negative. You can't say ខ្ញុំមិនមានទេ for "I don't have any" — the correct form is ខ្ញុំគ្មានទេ. It is a word of its own, not មិន + មាន.
**មែនទេ?** (*mèn-té?*) at the end of a sentence means "right?", "isn't it?" — a tag question used just as often as in English.

grammars.title: Answering without saying "yes"
body: In Khmer, the "yes" answer to a question with a verb is to **repeat the verb**. English does this too: "Are you going?" "I am." "Can you?" "I can." You just carry the habit over.

after: បាទ and ចាស can be added in front of your answer as politeness words — បាទ ទៅ — but on their own they often feel thin, like answering "yes" without saying yes to what. Repeating the verb always sounds more Cambodian.

sections.title: Saying no politely without sounding cold

blocks.text: A Cambodian host will offer food, drinks, and a seat again and again. A flat អត់ទេ feels stiff. The following sentences decline while staying warm, and all of them are used every day.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Three refusals to prepare now
items: **Alcohol.** Turning down beer in Cambodia needs a clear sentence, because the offer will come again and again: ខ្ញុំមិនផឹកស្រាទេ (*khnyom min pheuk sraa té*). Adding a religious reason — ខ្ញុំជាមូស្លីម (*khnyom chiè muu-sliim*, "I'm Muslim") — usually closes the topic respectfully rather than awkwardly.

**Pork.** ខ្ញុំមិនញ៉ាំសាច់ជ្រូកទេ (*khnyom min nyam sach-chruuk té*). Covered in more detail in unit 7 — but if it matters to you, memorize this sentence now, because you will need it before unit 7 arrives.
**Photos.** If you don't want your picture taken: សូមកុំថតរូបខ្ញុំ (*soum kom that ruup khnyom*), "please don't photograph me". សូម in front makes the prohibition sound like a request, not an order.
